newsitem.title: BELARUS: Outgoing U.S. envoy says fears for Belarus reforms.
newsitem.headline: Outgoing U.S. envoy says fears for Belarus reforms.

text.p: Washington's outgoing envoy to Belarus said on Monday he was concerned at the slow pace of reforms in the former Soviet republic and urged Minsk to strike up a new loan deal with the International Monetary Fund.
"I am leaving Belarus anxious that Belarus is not moving fast enough on reforms," Kenneth Yalovitz told a news conference through an interpreter on the eve of his departure.

He said the United States, which has advised investors to put their money into neighbouring states rather than Belarus, had not changed its policy on the country of 10 million, whose President Alexander Lukashenko is seeking closer ties with Russia.
"Our policy right now is that we unfortunately are not able to encourage our companies to invest in you," Yalovitz said.

Minsk's relations with Washington have been strained in recent years, especially since the U.S. embassy's first secretary Serzh Alexandrov was briefly detained at an opposition rally in March and expelled.
Washington said Alexandrov was carrying out normal diplomatic duties by observing a demonstration and gave his opposite number in Washington 24 hours to leave.
Lukashenko accused the West of funding the opposition and waging a campaign to disrupt his drive for union with Russia.
The United States has also cut $40 million in aid to Belarus over its human rights record.
The IMF still hold regular meetings with Belarussian economic officials but its $250 million stand-by arrangement with the country was frozen in 1995 pending faster reforms.
"Belarus must again come to an agreement with the International Monetary Fund on macroeconomic stabilisation and restructuring, and fulfil it," Yalovitz said.
Interfax news agency quoted Lukashenko as saying at a meeting with Yalovitz earlier on Monday that Washington's policy on Belarus was "too harsh".

Lukashenko enjoys wide support at home if not in the West, where he comes under constant criticism especially for a referendum last November in which he used a landslide win to rewrite the constitution, awarding himself sweeping powers.
